sentences.text: Scolosaurus is an extinct genus of two known species of medium-sized ankylosaurian thyreophoran dinosaurs that lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous.
This ankylosaur had a body length of about 6 meters and a weight of about 2 tons.
The type species, Scolosaurus cutleri, grew up to 5.6 meters long and weighed 2.2 metric tons.
The holotype torso of Scolosaurus is nearly completely intact.
It is the only North American ankylosaur specimen where the armor position can be determined with certainty.
The holotype specimen preserves rare osteoderms and skin impressions.
The animal possesses backswept squamosal horns with distinct tips that are proportionately longer than in related species.
The tail club knob of Scolosaurus appears circular when viewed from above.
Scolosaurus was first described by Franz Nopcsa in 1928.
Nopcsa von Felső-Szilvás named the dinosaur based on holotype NHMUK R.5161.
The holotype specimen of Scolosaurus is NHMUK PV R.5161, housed in the Natural History Museum in London.
The holotype skeleton was discovered by collector William Edmund Cutler in 1914 at Deadlodge Canyon.
Specimen USNM 7943 was excavated by G. M. Dawson in 1874 from the Frenchman Formation in Alberta.
There are four recorded fossil occurrences of Scolosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
Scolosaurus has nostrils that face forward.
Scolosaurus is classified as an ankylosaurid dinosaur in the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.
Scolosaurus belongs to the tribe Euoplocephalini.
In 1971, Walter Coombs synonymized the genera Anodontosaurus, Dyoplosaurus, and Scolosaurus with Euoplocephalus tutus.
In 1928, Nopcsa assigned the specimen to the family Ankylosauridae and made morphological comparisons with known Dyoplosaurus fossil material.
Researchers distinguish Scolosaurus from Euoplocephalus based on cervical armor, general armor details, and forelimb structure.
Scolosaurus differs from Anodontosaurus lambei and Euoplocephalus tutus in having a horn on the squamosal that is relatively longer, more posterior, and with a prominent tip.
Scolosaurus differs from Euoplocephalus tutus in having small, fused, and rounded dermal ossifications at the bases of the squamosal and quadratojugal.
Scolosaurus fossils are found in the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
It was collected from the bottom of the Dinosaur Park Formation, deposited during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 76.5 million years ago.
Scolosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The habitat of Scolosaurus featured a seasonal, semi-arid climate with warm temperatures and long dry seasons.
Volcanic eruptions periodically blanketed the Scolosaurus habitat with ash, causing mass mortality but also enriching the soil for plant growth.
Fluctuating sea levels created diverse environments for Scolosaurus, including marine habitats, coastal wetlands, deltas, lagoons, and inland floodplains.
A 2013 redescription by Paul Penkalski and William T. Blows suggests the genus is a valid taxon.
However, this synonymization is controversial because Oohkotokia was later recognized as valid.
Penkalski and Blows are thought to have identified two differences between Scolosaurus and Oohkotokia, stating that lateral projections of tail vertebrae are longer in Oohkotokia.

Arbour believed a significant comparison between Scolosaurus and Oohkotokia was impossible because only one tail vertebra is known in MOR 433, making it impossible to determine the position of that vertebra and how relative length varies with position.
It is debated whether the genus Oohkotokia is synonymous with Scolosaurus.
A 2015 phylogenetic analysis by Victoria Arbor and Phillip J. Currie placed Scolosaurus within a specific clade of Ankylosaurinae.
